rules.statement: When a management operation targets a route-addressed tenant and drives protocol machinery (issuing grants, signing tokens, back-channel logout), run it on a context materialized for that addressed tenant, not on the request's ambient OpenID context.
rules.why: The ambient context carries the request-resolved tenant (the management host), so using it would key grants and sign logout tokens in the wrong tenant's security domain.
rules.check: Look for admin/management endpoints under a {tenantId} route that pass the request's ambient OpenIdContext (or its Tenant/Mediator) to session, grant or token services instead of a context created for the route tenant.

rules.statement: Treat a secondary context materialized for an explicit tenant as caller-owned: dispose it (e.g. with a using declaration) and never publish it as the ambient request feature.
rules.why: It is a secondary context distinct from the request's own; publishing it would replace the request's tenant identity, and the caller owns its lifetime.
rules.check: Look for explicitly created tenant contexts that are not disposed, or that are set into HttpContext.Features or another ambient accessor.

rules.statement: Do not read from or write to the shared request-materialized tenant cache when materializing a tenant by explicit id; materialize it fresh.
rules.why: Cached tenants take their base address from the request host. Mixing them with issuer-derived admin materializations, in either direction, causes correctness bugs. Admin operations are rare, so the extra cost is acceptable.
rules.check: Look for by-id or explicit-tenant materialization code that probes, populates or shares the tenant cache used by request-driven tenant resolution.

rules.statement: When materializing a tenant independently of a request, use the tenant's own configured issuer as its identity and base address, and fail fast if no issuer is configured rather than deriving one from the current request host.
rules.why: There is no inbound request for that tenant to derive a host from. Falling back to the request host would make the tenant's identity vary by request and sign under the wrong issuer.
rules.check: Look for explicit-tenant materialization that falls back to HttpContext.Request host/scheme for the issuer or base address, or that quietly continues when the issuer setting is missing.

rules.statement: Implement admin session revocation by delegating to the context-bound session service's termination path, not by deleting or revoking grants directly in the store.
rules.why: Going directly to the store skips the termination seam, so back-channel logout is never sent to relying parties and no per-session audit runs.
rules.check: Look for admin endpoints that call store bulk-revoke/delete methods (e.g. RevokeWhereAsync) for sessions instead of ISessionService.RevokeAsync/RevokeAllAsync on an addressed-tenant context.

rules.statement: Keep tenant-bound services context-bound; to target another tenant, materialize a context for it instead of adding tenant-id-parameterized overloads.
rules.why: Overloads fork the service surface, and downstream machinery still needs a materialized tenant to sign under, so they collapse into context materialization anyway.
rules.check: Look for new overloads on context-bound services that take a tenantId parameter to bypass the bound context.

rules.statement: Record administrator-initiated session revocations in the management audit, attributed to the acting administrator, in addition to the per-session protocol audit.
rules.why: The admin action has to be traceable to whoever performed it, separately from the per-session audit that the termination seam records.
rules.check: Look for admin revoke endpoints that do not record a management audit event identifying the acting administrator.
